sections.name: Cloud Security (AWS, Azure, GCP)
sections.explanation_simple: Cloud security is about protecting your data and applications when they run on someone else's computers (AWS, Azure, Google Cloud). The most important concept is the 'shared responsibility model': the cloud provider secures the physical servers and network, but YOU are responsible for securing your data, access permissions, and configurations. Most cloud breaches happen because of MISCONFIGURATION - someone leaves an S3 bucket public, gives too many permissions to a user, or forgets to enable encryption. The cloud isn't insecure by default, but it's incredibly easy to accidentally make it insecure.
key_concepts: Shared Responsibility Model: Cloud provider secures the cloud, you secure what's IN the cloud
IAM (Identity and Access Management): Who can do what in your cloud account
Least Privilege: Give minimum permissions needed (most cloud breaches = too many permissions)
S3 Bucket: AWS storage (famous for being accidentally left public - the #1 cloud breach)
CloudTrail: AWS's audit log of every action in your account (critical for forensics)
GuardDuty: AWS's threat detection service (ML-based anomaly detection)
Security Groups: Virtual firewalls for EC2 instances (stateful, allow rules only)
NACLs: Network Access Control Lists for subnets (stateless, allow AND deny rules)
KMS: Key Management Service (manages encryption keys)
Cloud HSM: Hardware Security Module (FIPS 140-2 Level 3 certified key storage)
VPC: Virtual Private Cloud (your isolated network in the cloud)
Azure AD: Microsoft's cloud identity service (like Active Directory but in the cloud)
GCP IAM: Google Cloud's permission system
CIS Benchmarks: Security configuration standards for cloud services

code_examples.title: AWS Security Audit with ScoutSuite
code_examples.code:
# ===== CLOUD SECURITY AUDIT =====
# ScoutSuite - Open-source multi-cloud security auditing tool
# Install: pip install scoutsuite

# Run an AWS audit:
# scout aws --report-dir ./reports

# This checks for:
# - S3 buckets with public access
# - IAM users with excessive permissions
# - Security groups with wide open ports (0.0.0.0/0)
# - CloudTrail not enabled
# - KMS keys not rotated
# - Unused security groups
# - Much more

"""

KEY CLOUD SECURITY CONFIGURATIONS:

1. S3 BUCKET SECURITY (THE most common mistake)
"""
# AWS CLI: Block public access
aws s3api put-public-access-block --bucket my-bucket --public-access-block-configuration "BlockPublicAcls=true,IgnorePublicAcls=true,BlockPublicPolicy=true,RestrictPublicBuckets=true"

# Check if a bucket is public:
aws s3api get-bucket-acl --bucket my-bucket

# Enable server-side encryption:
aws s3api put-bucket-encryption --bucket my-bucket --server-side-encryption-configuration '{"Rules":[{"ApplyServerSideEncryptionByDefault":{"SSEAlgorithm":"AES256"}}]}'

# Enable bucket versioning (to recover from ransomware):
aws s3api put-bucket-versioning --bucket my-bucket --versioning-configuration Status=Enabled

"""
2. IAM BEST PRACTICES
"""
# IAM policy with least privilege:
# This allows an EC2 instance to ONLY read from a specific S3 bucket
{
    "Version": "2012-10-17",
    "Statement": [
        {
            "Effect": "Allow",
            "Action": [
                "s3:GetObject",
                "s3:ListBucket"
            ],
            "Resource": [
                "arn:aws:s3:::my-app-data",
                "arn:aws:s3:::my-app-data/*"
            ],
            "Condition": {
                "IpAddress": {
                    "aws:SourceIp": "10.0.0.0/16"
                }
            }
        },
        {
            "Effect": "Deny",
            "Action": "s3:DeleteObject",
            "Resource": "arn:aws:s3:::my-app-data/*",
            "Condition": {
                "Bool": {
                    "aws:SecureTransport": "false"
                }
            }
        }
    ]
}

# Create IAM role (NOT a user!) for applications:
aws iam create-role --role-name MyAppRole --assume-role-policy-document file://trust-policy.json

# Attach the policy:
aws iam put-role-policy --role-name MyAppRole --policy-name S3ReadAccess --policy-document file://s3-access.json

"""
3. VPC SECURITY
"""
# Security group: Web server (only 80/443 from anywhere, SSH only from office)
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id sg-12345 --protocol tcp --port 80 --cidr 0.0.0.0/0
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id sg-12345 --protocol tcp --port 443 --cidr 0.0.0.0/0
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id sg-12345 --protocol tcp --port 22 --cidr 203.0.113.0/24  # OFFICE IP

# Database security group (ONLY from web servers):
aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id sg-db --protocol tcp --port 3306 --source-group sg-12345

# NEVER do this:
# aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress --group-id sg-db --protocol tcp --port 3306 --cidr 0.0.0.0/0  # NO!

sections.name: Container & Kubernetes Security
sections.explanation_simple: Container security is about protecting Docker and Kubernetes deployments. Containers are like lightweight VMs that package an application with everything it needs to run. Kubernetes (k8s) orchestrates thousands of containers across multiple machines. Container security issues include: using vulnerable base images, running containers as root, not setting resource limits (one container can DoS the whole host), and misconfiguring Kubernetes RBAC (giving too many permissions). The golden rule: containers should run with the absolute minimum privileges needed.
key_concepts: Image Scanning: Checking container images for known vulnerabilities (Trivy, Clair, Snyk)
Docker Bench Security: CIS benchmark checker for Docker hosts
Container Escape: Breaking out of a container to access the host OS (critical vulnerability)
Privileged Container: Container with ALL capabilities (never do this in production!)
ReadOnly Root Filesystem: Container's filesystem is read-only (prevents malware writing files)
Kubernetes RBAC: Who can do what in K8s (namespaces, roles, bindings)
Pod Security Policies: Rules for what pods can do (deprecated, replaced by OPA/Gatekeeper)
OPA/Gatekeeper: Policy engine for Kubernetes (enforce security rules)
Service Mesh: mTLS between services (Istio, Linkerd - encrypts all pod-to-pod traffic)
Secrets Management: Storing and accessing secrets in K8s (don't put them in YAML!)
Network Policies: Firewall rules between pods (micro-segmentation)
Admission Controllers: Validate/deny pod creation based on security rules
Runtime Security: Monitoring containers for suspicious activity (Falco, Sysdig)
Supply Chain Security: Ensuring the images you use haven't been tampered with (Sigstore, Cosign)
Namespaces: Isolating different environments/users in K8s

code_examples.title: Docker & Kubernetes Security Hardening
code_examples.code:
# ===== DOCKER SECURITY BEST PRACTICES =====

"""
1. DOCKERFILE SECURITY
"""
# BAD Dockerfile:
FROM ubuntu:latest
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl wget
COPY . /app
RUN chmod -R 777 /app
USER root
CMD ["./app"]

# GOOD Dockerfile:
FROM ubuntu:22.04 AS builder
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends curl \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
COPY . /app
RUN make build

FROM ubuntu:22.04  # Fresh minimal image
RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends \
    ca-certificates \
    && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
COPY --from=builder /app/bin /app/

# Security hardening
RUN addgroup --gid 1001 --system appgroup && \
    adduser --uid 1001 --system --ingroup appgroup --no-create-home appuser
USER appuser:appgroup  # NOT root!

# Read-only root filesystem
# docker run --read-only --tmpfs /tmp ...

# Drop all capabilities
# docker run --cap-drop ALL --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE ...

# Use specific tag (not :latest!)
FROM python:3.11-slim@sha256:xxxxx

# Health check
HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=3s --retries=3 CMD curl -f http://localhost:8080/health || exit 1

WORKDIR /app
ENTRYPOINT ["/app/app"]

"""
2. DOCKER RUN SECURITY
"""
# Scan image for vulnerabilities:
# trivy image myapp:latest

# Run with security options:
docker run -d \
    --name myapp \
    --read-only \
    --tmpfs /tmp:rw,noexec,nosuid,size=100M \
    --cap-drop ALL \
    --cap-add NET_BIND_SERVICE \
    --security-opt=no-new-privileges \
    --security-opt=seccomp=default.json \
    --pids-limit 100 \
    --memory 512m \
    --cpus 1 \
    myapp:1.0.0

# Run Docker Bench Security audit:
# docker run --rm --net host --pid host --userns host \
#     --cap-add audit_control \
#     -e DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST=$DOCKER_CONTENT_TRUST \
#     -v /var/lib:/var/lib \
#     -v /var/run/docker.sock:/var/run/docker.sock \
#     -v /etc:/etc \
#     docker/docker-bench-security

"""
3. KUBERNETES SECURITY
"""
#------
# Namespace isolation
#------
kubectl create namespace production
kubectl create namespace staging
kubectl create namespace development

# Resource quota (prevent DoS)
apiVersion: v1
kind: ResourceQuota
metadata:
  name: prod-quota
  namespace: production
spec:
  hard:
    requests.cpu: '10'
    requests.memory: 20Gi
    limits.cpu: '20'
    limits.memory: 40Gi
---

#------
# Pod Security (runAsNonRoot, readOnlyRootFilesystem)
#------
apiVersion: v1
kind: Pod
metadata:
  name: secure-pod
spec:
  securityContext:
    runAsNonRoot: true
    runAsUser: 1001
    fsGroup: 1001
  containers:
  - name: myapp
    image: myapp:1.0.0
    securityContext:
      allowPrivilegeEscalation: false
      readOnlyRootFilesystem: true
      capabilities:
        drop: ["ALL"]
        add: ["NET_BIND_SERVICE"]
    resources:
      requests:
        memory: "256Mi"
        cpu: "250m"
      limits:
        memory: "512Mi"
        cpu: "500m"
---

#------
# Network Policy (deny all ingress by default)
#------
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: default-deny
  namespace: production
spec:
  podSelector: {}
  policyTypes:
  - Ingress
---

# Allow only api-gateway to access backend
apiVersion: networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: NetworkPolicy
metadata:
  name: allow-api-to-backend
spec:
  podSelector:
    matchLabels:
      app: backend
  ingress:
  - from:
    - podSelector:
        matchLabels:
          app: api-gateway
    ports:
    - port: 8080
---

#------
# Falco: Runtime security monitoring
#------
# Falco detects anomalous container behavior
# Install: helm install falco falcosecurity/falco
# Detect rules:
# - Shell inside container (potential container escape)
# - Kubernetes client inside container
# - Outbound network connection to suspicious IPs
# - File write to /etc (potential config tampering)

# Example Falco rule (yaml):
- rule: Terminal shell in container
  desc: A shell was spawned in a container
  condition: container and proc.name = bash
  output: "Shell spawned (user=%user.name container=%container.name shell=%proc.name pid=%proc.pid)"
  priority: WARNING

sections.name: API Security & Secure Development
sections.explanation_simple: API security is about protecting the interfaces that applications use to talk to each other. Most modern apps are powered by APIs - every time you use a mobile app, it's talking to an API server. API security covers authentication (who are you?), authorization (what can you do?), input validation (are you sending bad data?), rate limiting (are you hammering the server?), and protection against common attacks like injection, broken authentication, and excessive data exposure. The OWASP API Security Top 10 is the go-to reference.
key_concepts: Authentication: Verifying identity (API keys, OAuth2, JWT, basic auth)
Authorization: What an authenticated user can access (RBAC, ABAC, scopes)
JWT (JSON Web Token): Self-contained token with claims (BEWARE: 'none' algorithm attacks!)
OAuth2: Authorization framework (delegated access, token-based)
OpenID Connect: Identity layer on top of OAuth2 (for authentication)
Rate Limiting: Limiting requests per user/IP to prevent abuse
API Gateway: Centralized entry point for APIs (handles auth, rate limiting, logging)
Input Validation: NEVER trust user input - validate, sanitize, and reject bad data
IDOR (Insecure Direct Object Reference): Changing an ID in the URL to access other users' data
Mass Assignment: Sending extra fields in a request to modify things you shouldn't
GraphQL Security: Query depth limiting, complexity analysis, proper authorization at resolver level
API Fuzzing: Sending random/malformed data to find vulnerabilities
Rate Limit Bypass: Techniques attackers use to bypass rate limits (IP rotation, headers)
Token Attacks: JWT alg confusion (RS256 -> HS256), token theft, token replay
CORS: Cross-Origin Resource Sharing - who can call your API from browsers

sections.name: IoT, Embedded & ICS/SCADA Security
sections.explanation_simple: IoT (Internet of Things) security covers all the connected devices around us - smart home devices, wearables, medical implants, industrial sensors, and cars. These devices are notoriously insecure because they're cheap (no budget for security), hard to update (no easy patching), and often have hardcoded passwords. ICS/SCADA (Industrial Control Systems) control critical infrastructure - power plants, water treatment, factories, pipelines. A hack of these systems can cause physical damage (like the 2015 Ukraine power grid hack or the Colonial Pipeline ransomware attack). Embedded security involves extracting firmware from chips (using UART/JTAG), analyzing code for vulnerabilities, and identifying hardcoded secrets.
key_concepts: Firmware: The software embedded in a device (stored in flash memory, often updatable)
Firmware Extraction: Reading the firmware from the device's flash memory (via UART, JTAG, or desoldering the chip)
UART: Universal Asynchronous Receiver/Transmitter - a serial port on circuit boards (often gives root shell!)
JTAG: Joint Test Action Group - debugging interface for embedded devices (full control of the CPU)
SPI Flash: Common memory chip used for firmware storage (can be read with a $10 programmer)
MQTT: Common IoT protocol (publish/subscribe messaging - often runs without authentication!)
CoAP: Constrained Application Protocol (HTTP-like for IoT devices)
Modbus: Industrial protocol (VERY old, no security built in - still widely used!)
DNP3: Another industrial protocol (slightly more secure than Modbus, still weak)
PLC: Programmable Logic Controller - the computer that controls industrial machinery
RTU: Remote Terminal Unit - field device in SCADA systems
HMI: Human-Machine Interface - the screen operators use to control industrial systems
Stuxnet: The most famous ICS attack - destroyed Iranian nuclear centrifuges in 2010
Trinity: The attack that disrupted Ukrainian power grid (2015)
Air Gap: A network physically isolated from the internet (Stuxnet proved it's not enough)
Hardcoded Credentials: Default passwords in IoT devices (admin/admin is still common!)
Firmware Analysis Tool: Binwalk (extracts files from firmware), Firmwalker (searches for secrets)
Hardware Hacking Tools: Bus Pirate, Saleae Logic Analyzer, FTDI Friend, CH341A programmer

code_examples.title: IoT Firmware Extraction & Analysis
code_examples.code:
# ===== FIRMWARE EXTRACTION & ANALYSIS =====
# Educational: Understanding IoT device security

"""
METHOD 1: READING SPI FLASH (most common)

Tools needed:
  - CH341A programmer ($10 on Amazon)
  - SOIC-8 clip (for in-circuit reading)
  - Flashrom software

Steps:
  1. Identify the SPI flash chip on the PCB (look for 8-pin chip with marking like "25Q128")
  2. Attach the SOIC-8 clip to the chip (align pin 1: dot on chip to red wire on clip)
  3. Connect clip to CH341A programmer
  4. Connect CH341A to USB
  5. Read the flash:

# flashrom -p ch341a_spi -r firmware.bin

# If chip not detected automatically:
# flashrom -p ch341a_spi -c "W25Q128.V" -r firmware.bin

METHOD 2: UART ACCESS (get a root shell!)

Steps:
  1. Find UART pins on PCB (look for 4 pins in a row, often labeled GND/TX/RX/VCC)
  2. Connect USB-to-UART adapter:
     - GND to GND
     - TX of adapter to RX of device
     - RX of adapter to TX of device
  3. Open serial terminal (115200 baud is common):

# screen /dev/ttyUSB0 115200

  4. Power on the device - you may get a boot console!
  5. Try pressing Enter during boot for U-Boot shell
  6. Look for: login prompts, boot messages, kernel panics (debug data!)
  7. Common default credentials: root/root, admin/admin, root/(empty)

METHOD 3: SOFTWARE-BASED EXTRACTION
  - Over-the-air (OTA) update: intercept the update binary
  - Web interface: download backup firmware
  - Vendor website: many provide firmware updates publicly
"""

# ===== FIRMWARE ANALYSIS =====

# 1. Analyze with binwalk
# binwalk firmware.bin  # Show embedded files
# binwalk -Me firmware.bin  # Extract all files

# 2. Search for secrets
# grep -r "password" extracted_firmware/
# grep -r "admin" extracted_firmware/
# grep -r "http://" extracted_firmware/
# grep -r "192.168." extracted_firmware/

# 3. Find filesystem
# strings firmware.bin | grep "squashfs"
# strings firmware.bin | grep "ext4"
# strings firmware.bin | grep "ubifs"

# 4. Extract filesystem
# dd if=firmware.bin bs=1 skip=<offset> of=rootfs.squashfs
# unsquashfs rootfs.squashfs

# 5. Analyze with firmwalker
# ./firmwalker.sh extracted_firmware/

# 6. Examine web interface files
# Look for: PHP backdoors, hardcoded API keys, command injection

# 7. Common IoT vulnerabilities to check:
# - Hardcoded SSH keys (look for id_rsa, dropbear)
# - Default certificates
# - Insecure update mechanism (no signature verification)
# - Command injection in web interface
# - Buffer overflow in network services (UPnP, HTTP)
# - Telnet enabled (still common!)
# - Outdated software (old OpenSSL, BusyBox)

# ===== ICS/SCADA PROTOCOLS =====

"""
Modbus Protocol (minimal security):
  - Function codes: 1 (read coils), 3 (read holding regs), 5 (write coil), 6 (write register)
  - NO authentication!   
  - NO encryption!
  - Just send a valid Modbus frame and the PLC obeys

DNP3 Protocol (slightly better):
  - Has authentication (Secure Authentication v5)
  - But many installations still use no auth

Common ICS Attacks:
  1. Modbus Injection: Write to coils/registers to change industrial process
  2. PLC Stop: Send stop command to PLC (can halt production)
  3. Data Manipulation: Change sensor readings (hide dangerous conditions)
  4. Ransomware: Encrypt PLC programs (at least 2 SCADA ransomware families exist)
"""

# Python: Modbus security scanner
from pymodbus.client import ModbusTcpClient
import sys

def scan_modbus_device(ip, port=502):
    """Check Modbus device for access to critical functions."""
    try:
        client = ModbusTcpClient(ip, port=port)
        client.connect()

        # Read coil 0 (often a critical control)
        result = client.read_coils(0, 1)
        if not result.isError():
            print(f"[!] Device at {ip}:{port} responds to Modbus")
            print(f"[!] Coil 0 value: {result.bits[0]}")
            print(f"[!] This means you could potentially write to coils (control industrial process)")

        # Try to read holding registers (often sensor data)
        result = client.read_holding_registers(0, 10)
        if not result.isError():
            print(f"[!] Holding registers 0-9: {result.registers}")

        client.close()
        return True

    except Exception as e:
        print(f"[-] No Modbus response from {ip}: {e}")
        return False

# Example:
# scan_modbus_device("192.168.1.100", 502)

sections.name: Identity & Access Security
sections.explanation_simple: Identity and access security is about making sure the right people have access to the right things in the right way. It's the most fundamental security control - if you can't control who has access to what, nothing else matters. Key concepts: SSO (Single Sign-On - one login for all services), MFA (Multi-Factor Authentication - something you know + something you have + something you are), Federation (trusting another organization's identity system), and PAM (Privileged Access Management - securing admin accounts). Identity attacks (phishing, MFA fatigue, token theft) are the #1 way attackers breach organizations today.
key_concepts: SSO: One login for all applications (SAML, OIDC, CAS)
MFA: Something you know (password) + something you have (phone) + something you are (fingerprint)
2FA: Two-factor authentication (subset of MFA)
TOTP: Time-based One-Time Password (Google Authenticator, Authy)
FIDO2/WebAuthn: Passwordless authentication (hardware security keys like YubiKey)
OAuth 2.0: Authorization framework (delegated access - "Login with Google")
OpenID Connect (OIDC): Authentication layer on top of OAuth 2.0
SAML: Security Assertion Markup Language (XML-based SSO, common in enterprises)
LDAP: Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (how apps look up users)
Federation: Trusting another organization's identity system (e.g., Login with Google, Microsoft)
SCIM: System for Cross-domain Identity Management (automatic user provisioning/deprovisioning)
PAM: Privileged Access Management (managing admin credentials, session recording)
RBAC: Role-Based Access Control (permissions based on job role)
ABAC: Attribute-Based Access Control (permissions based on user/resource attributes)
MFA Fatigue: Attackers keep pushing MFA prompts until user accepts (very effective!)
Token Theft: Stealing session tokens to bypass authentication entirely
Passwordless: Authentication without passwords (using biometrics, security keys, or magic links)
